title: Indian American Voters Lean Democratic as Trump Approval Falls Before Midterms
excerpt: Two 2026 surveys show 66% of Indian American voters backing Democratic congressional candidates and 71% disapproving of Trump, even as independent identification climbs to 29%.
body:
• 66% of Indian American voters back Democratic candidates in both Senate and House races in the 2026 Asian American Voter Survey, against 22% for Republicans in Senate races and 18% in House races.
  • 71% of Indian Americans disapprove of President Trump's job performance in Carnegie's 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey, with 64% disapproving of his immigration policy.
  • Turnout intent is high: 92% of Indian American registered voters plan to vote in the November midterms, and 74% say they are absolutely certain they will.
  • For voters still deciding: all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate are on the ballot, and 29% of Indian Americans now identify as independents — the bloc both parties are chasing in the final days.

Eight days before the November midterm elections, the surveys point in one direction: President Donald Trump's gains among Indian American voters in 2024 have not held. According to the 2026 Asian American Voter Survey by APIAVote and AAPI Data, 66 per cent of Indian American voters support Democratic candidates in Senate races, compared with 22 per cent for Republicans. In House races the split is 66 per cent to 18 per cent. Indian Americans recorded the highest Democratic Senate support of any major Asian ethnic group in the survey.

The view of the president himself is sharper. Seventy-four per cent of Indian American respondents in the AAPI survey viewed Trump unfavourably, including 56 per cent who held a very unfavourable opinion, against 20 per cent who viewed him favourably. The 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, conducted with YouGov among 1,000 Indian American adults, found 71 per cent disapproved of Trump's job performance in the first year of his second term and only 29 per cent approved.

What changed since 2024

Trump improved his standing with Indian Americans in 2024. Carnegie's 2024 survey found 61 per cent of registered Indian American voters intended to vote for Kamala Harris and 31 per cent for Trump, up from 22 per cent for Trump in 2020. The 2026 data suggest that shift was not locked in. Carnegie found Trump's support among Indian American men aged 18 to 39 fell from 40 per cent in 2024 to 24 per cent in 2026, according to reporting on the survey.

"Bottom line: API voters favor Democratic candidates over Republican candidates when we look at it in the Senate or the House."

— Karthick Ramakrishnan, AAPI Data

The issues driving the shift

Cost of living dominates. In the AAPI survey, 90 per cent of Asian American voters rated cost of living and inflation as very or extremely important, followed by healthcare at 82 per cent, jobs and unemployment at 80 per cent, and Social Security and Medicare at 80 per cent. On cost of living, 44 per cent said Democrats would do a better job, against 18 per cent for Republicans — though 36 per cent said neither party was better, a persuadable group both campaigns still have time to reach.

Immigration carries specific weight in this community. Carnegie found 64 per cent of Indian Americans disapprove of Trump's immigration policy, and 66 per cent opposed the $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions, a policy that falls heavily on Indian nationals, who make up the largest share of H-1B workers. Carnegie also found 55 per cent disapproved of Trump's handling of US-India relations, against 20 per cent who approved, and majorities disapproved of his handling of the domestic economy and of trade and tariffs.

Not a simple swing back

The data do not show a clean return to the Democrats. Democratic identification among Indian Americans fell from 52 per cent in 2020 to 46 per cent in 2026, while Republican identification rose from 15 per cent to 19 per cent and independents climbed to 29 per cent, up from 23 per cent in 2020. The Democratic Party's favourability also slipped, from 60 in 2024 to 53 in 2026. As GG2's analysis of the surveys put it, three things are happening at once: weaker Democratic identification, a still-smaller but growing Republican constituency, and a larger independent bloc.

Outreach remains thin. About a third of AAPI registered voters said neither major party had contacted them in the past year — 42 per cent reported no contact from Democrats and 58 per cent none from Republicans.

Why the numbers matter on November 3

There are about 2.6 million eligible Indian American voters, and they are concentrated in states and suburbs where margins are thin — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Georgia, Texas and New Jersey among them. The wider AAPI electorate totals 16 million eligible voters in 2026, including 1.6 million newly eligible since 2022. With 92 per cent of Indian American registered voters planning to vote and enthusiasm up more than in any other major Asian ethnic group surveyed, even a modest shift in this electorate can decide close House districts. What to watch on election night is not only which party Indian Americans back, but whether the growing independent share turns out at the same rate as the partisans.
